recall.define: Define release time, response time, jitter, worst-case execution time, period and deadline without the glossary and name the source for each.
recall.distinguish: Give the distinction and a numeric example for: latency versus response time; measured maximum versus worst-case execution time; period versus deadline; preemptive scheduler versus cooperative scheduler; tick versus tickless timing.
recall.apply: A sensor task with a 10 ms period misses its deadline once an hour. Using release time, response time, jitter, interrupt latency and measured maximum, state which measurement separates a scheduling cause from an interrupt-masking cause, why a day of measurements still does not establish a worst-case execution time, and which term names the quantity the watchdog actually bounds.

entries.definition: The instant at which a job of a periodic or event-driven task becomes ready to run; the reference point from which latency and response time are measured, which a timer-driven system must record independently of when the job actually starts.
idiom: release latency is start minus release; response is finish minus release
entries.misconception: A job's release time is when it starts executing.

entries.definition: The interval from a job's release to its completion, including waiting for higher-priority work and its own execution; the quantity compared against the deadline in response-time analysis.

distinguish_from.distinction: Latency ends when the handler or task starts; response time ends when the required work is finished.

entries.definition: The variation of a timing quantity (release, start or completion) between successive jobs relative to the ideal periodic instants; it is a distribution, reported with its maximum and its source, not a single number.

authority.locator: C1.8.3 CYCCNT cycle counter and related timers — CYCCNT definition and profiling notes

entries.misconception: Jitter is noise that averages out.

entries.definition: An upper bound on the execution time of a code path over all inputs and hardware states, established by analysis or exhaustive argument; a measured maximum is a lower bound on it and never a substitute. Written WCET after its first use.

authority.locator: C1.8.3 CYCCNT cycle counter and related timers — CYCCNT definition and profiling notes

distinguish_from.distinction: The largest value seen in a campaign; it depends on the inputs exercised and says nothing about unobserved paths or cache states.

entries.misconception: Running the task for a day gives its WCET.

entries.definition: The largest value of a timing quantity observed in a recorded campaign, reported with its inputs, clock, build identity and uncertainty; evidence about that campaign only.
entries.misconception: A measured maximum with a safety margin is a bound.

entries.definition: The fixed interval between successive releases of a periodic task; the deadline is often but not necessarily equal to it, and the period, not the execution time, determines how much processor time the task demands.
entries.misconception: Calling delay(10) at the end of the loop gives a 10 ms period (it gives 10 ms plus the execution time).

entries.definition: The latest acceptable completion time of a job relative to its release; a hard deadline makes a late result worthless or dangerous, a soft one degrades value. Scheduling analysis compares worst-case response time against it.
entries.misconception: Meeting deadlines in testing proves schedulability.

entries.definition: The simplest firmware structure: one infinite loop that polls inputs and runs each activity in turn, with interrupts only setting flags; its response time is bounded by the sum of all activities, which is why it stops scaling.
entries.misconception: A superloop has no concurrency problems (interrupt handlers still share state with it).

entries.definition: A scheduler in which a task runs until it yields or blocks; switches happen only at known points, which removes most data races between tasks but makes response time depend on the longest run between yields.

distinguish_from.distinction: A preemptive scheduler switches tasks on timer or interrupt events at arbitrary points, bounding response time but reintroducing shared-state hazards.

entries.misconception: Cooperative scheduling is always simpler and safer.

entries.definition: A scheduler that can suspend the running task at any instruction boundary in favor of a higher-priority ready task, usually from a tick or interrupt handler through PendSV on Cortex-M; every shared datum then needs explicit synchronization.

Saving the running task's registers and stack pointer and restoring another task's, on Cortex-M split between the hardware exception frame and the software-saved callee registers in PendSV; its cost and its interaction with the floating-point context are measurable dispatch overheads.
entries.misconception: A context switch is free on a microcontroller.

entries.definition: The periodic timer interrupt that advances the scheduler's notion of time and drives time slicing and delays; tick resolution bounds the precision of timeouts, and a tickless mode suppresses ticks during idle to save power at the cost of wakeup bookkeeping.
entries.misconception: Timeouts are accurate to the tick period (they are accurate to within one tick plus jitter).

entries.definition: The return of a free-running counter to zero after its maximum; comparisons of absolute timestamps break at the wrap, while unsigned differences modulo the counter width remain correct as long as intervals are shorter than half the range.
entries.misconception: A 32-bit millisecond counter never wraps in practice (it wraps after about 49.7 days).

entries.definition: A hardware timer that resets the device unless software refreshes it within a window; it bounds the time the system can stay unresponsive, not the correctness of what it does, and a refresh placed in a timer handler defeats it.
entries.misconception: Refreshing the watchdog from an interrupt proves the main loop is alive.

entries.definition: Establishing the maximum stack use of a task from the call graph and per-function frame sizes (compiler -fstack-usage reports) plus interrupt nesting, rather than from a fill-pattern high-water mark observed in testing.
entries.misconception: The high-water mark after a test run is the stack requirement.

entries.definition: The lost-wakeup hazard in which a task checks for pending work, finds none, and enters a low-power wait after the interrupt that would have woken it has already fired; closed by checking the condition with interrupts masked and using an instruction (WFE/WFI) that honors events that arrived during the check.

authority.locator: B1.5.17 Power management — WFE and WFI
